source_refs.note: Four Basic Types of Gws: a main subheading of 8.6 Gravitational waves (GWs), its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 183-183.

blocks.text: There are four basic types of gravitational waves, each with different sources and characteristics:
When a single massive object spins with a constant rate, such as a neutron star, continuous GWs are produced with the same frequency and amplitude. White dwarf binary systems produce continuous Gws.
When a binary system, such as binary neutron stars, binary black holes, or a neutron star and black hole orbiting each other, compact inspirational GWs are produced.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints “Inspirational”. The term is compact binary inspiral GWs: the two objects spiral in towards each other (inspiral) as they lose energy to gravitational waves.
These are produced by violent events like supernovae, gamma-ray bursts, or cosmic strings.

blocks.text: Stochastic GWs are weak, random signals of GWs which are produced by superposition of many weak gravitational wave sources, such as distant binary systems. These GWs are the most difficult to detect.

Every physical object that accelerates, produces gravitational waves. Vehicles, airplanes, etc. are included in it. The masses and acceleration of objects on the Earth are too small to make gravitational waves big enough to be detected with our instruments.

As the binary systems (also termed as binaries) orbit each other, they emit gravitational waves, which can be detected by observatories like LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational wave Observatory) which is situated in USA and Virgo, a large scale gravitational wave observatory in Cascina, Italy. The waves carry information about the system's mass, spin, and merger dynamics, offering insights into these extreme cosmic objects, and move with the speed of light.

blocks.alt: On a dark blue starry sky, several sets of pale blue-white concentric rings, seen at a slant, each with a small binary pair at its centre; the Earth is at the lower left.
blocks.caption: Picture of a series of concentric spheres, with the binary system at the center, radiating gravity waves outward into the cosmos (original drawing after the picture printed in the textbook).

blocks.text: The binary systems are significant sources of gravitational waves, and their mergers (collision and union of two massive objects resulting more massive single object) are among the most intense cosmic events.

As the masses orbit and accelerate, their gravitational intensity fluctuates, generating waves that radiate outward in all directions. These waves are not bound by the binary system's gravity; instead, they travel freely through spacetime at the speed of light. The waves propagate through the universe, weakening in intensity as they distance themselves from the source.
